title: The academy of Gondishapur

traditional.note: Later Arabic writers credit the Sasanian king Khosrow I with founding a university, medical school and hospital at Gondishapur around 555.

confidence.note: The city's founding by Shapur I and the 8th-century careers of its Christian doctors in Baghdad are reasonably documented. Almost everything said about a school or hospital there comes from Arabic writers of the 12th and 13th centuries, and scholars disagree over whether a formal academy ever existed.

summary: A Persian city of Christian doctors that later writers turned into a legendary medical university. How much of the legend is true is still argued.
body: Shapur I built Gondishapur, known in Syriac as Beth Lapat, as a planned city in southwest Iran and settled it with Graeco-Syrian prisoners taken in his victory over the Roman emperor Valerian in 260. By the 8th century its Christian doctors were famous: in 765, later biographers say, Jurjis ibn Bakhtishu left the hospital he ran there for the caliph's court in Baghdad. The grander picture, of a university and teaching hospital founded by Khosrow I, rests on writers of the 12th and 13th centuries. Some Western historians call it a myth promoted by the Bakhtishu family; Touraj Nayernouri defends it from Syriac Christian texts.

myth.tradition: Gondishapur was a great medical university and teaching hospital founded by Khosrow I around 555, the model for later Islamic hospitals.
myth.record: Contemporary texts about the place are scarce, and the accounts of a university and teaching hospital were written centuries later. Even sceptics generally accept that a hospital existed, but its founding, size and role as a model for Baghdad's hospital are disputed; Nayernouri argues from earlier Syriac texts that a medical school did exist.

links.note: Physicians from Gondishapur, such as the Bakhtishus and Ibn Masawayh, moved to Baghdad, where Ibn Masawayh taught Hunayn.
Whether Baghdad's first hospital copied Gondishapur is part of the same dispute.

title: The translation movement of Baghdad

confidence.note: The translations themselves survive, and Hunayn ibn Ishaq described his own method in a letter that still exists. That translation began under al-Mansur and blossomed in the first two Abbasid centuries is the scholarly consensus; the exact end point is a convention, and the role of the 'House of Wisdom' is the part that is contested.

people: al-Mansur (r. 754–775), caliph who founded Baghdad and sponsored the first translations
Ibn al-Muqaffa' (d. 756), secretary and translator from Middle Persian
Hunayn ibn Ishaq (808–873), Christian physician and the movement's greatest translator
Ishaq ibn Hunayn (d. 910), his son and fellow translator
summary: For two centuries Baghdad's scholars turned Greek, Persian and Indian learning into Arabic. Almost all of Galen came through one Christian translator's workshop.
body: Between the mid-8th and the 10th century, scholars in Abbasid Iraq turned a large part of Greek medicine, science and philosophy into Arabic. The first translations of the Abbasid era were made under al-Mansur (r. 754–775), the caliph who founded Baghdad in 762, and the work blossomed over the next two centuries. Many translators were Syriac-speaking Christians, heirs to a late antique habit of studying Greek texts in Syriac, and their patrons ranged from caliphs to court physicians and wealthy lords who competed to acquire manuscripts.

The central figure was Hunayn ibn Ishaq (808–873), a Christian from al-Hira whose father was a pharmacist. Trained in Baghdad under the physician Yuhanna ibn Masawayh, he and his circle, including his son Ishaq and his nephew Hubaysh, put well over a hundred Greek medical works into Syriac or Arabic: Hippocrates, Dioscorides and almost the entire corpus of Galen. In a letter listing his Galen translations, Hunayn describes searching Mesopotamia, Syria, Palestine and Egypt for manuscripts, collating several copies of a work, and translating for sense rather than word for word. He helped create the technical vocabulary of scientific Arabic.

Greek was not the only source. Ibn al-Muqaffa', secretary under al-Mansur, is credited with Arabic versions of Middle Persian works, though the attribution of one, a compendium of logic, is disputed. Indian medicine arrived too: al-Razi's vast compilation, the *Hawi*, preserves fragments of Sanskrit authorities such as Sushruta and Caraka. The formulary of Sabur ibn Sahl, compiled at Gondishapur in the 9th century and used in Baghdad's hospitals, shows Persian, Greek and Indian medicine blended.

The best-known image of the movement is the 'House of Wisdom' (*Bayt al-hikma*), pictured as a state academy of translators. It was a real court library, but it cannot be viewed as an institutional center of translation, which had many sponsors and began decades before it. What is not in doubt is the reach of the result: it was largely through Arabic that medieval Europe later recovered Galen and Hippocrates.

myth.tradition: The House of Wisdom, under the caliph al-Ma'mun in the early 9th century, was an academy built to translate Greek science, and the movement was run from there.
myth.record: The House of Wisdom was a court library. Translation had begun under al-Mansur decades earlier and was paid for by many patrons, from caliphs to physicians and lords; the library cannot be viewed as an institutional center of translation.

title: The bimaristans

confidence.note: That large endowed hospitals spread across the Islamic world from the 9th century is well documented. The founding of Baghdad's first hospital under Harun al-Rashid rests on later biographers, who disagree over whether the caliph or his vizier founded it, and earlier claims such as a Damascus hospital of 707 are contested.

place: Baghdad, then Cairo, Damascus and other cities
people: Harun al-Rashid (r. 786–809), caliph under whom Baghdad's first hospital was founded
Yahya ibn Khalid, Persian vizier sometimes credited with the foundation
Jibrail ibn Bakhtishu, Christian physician who headed the first Baghdad hospital
Ahmad ibn Tulun, Abbasid governor of Egypt who built a hospital in 872
'Ali ibn 'Isa, Baghdad vizier who extended hospital care in the 920s and 930s
summary: Endowed hospitals with wards, pharmacies and teaching physicians, open to Muslims and non-Muslims alike, spread from Baghdad across the Islamic world.
body: The *bimaristan* (from Persian *bimar*, 'sick person', and *stan*, 'place') was the hospital of the medieval Islamic world. Baghdad's first was founded around 800, either at the order of the caliph Harun al-Rashid (r. 786–809) or of his Persian vizier Yahya ibn Khalid, and was headed by Jibrail ibn Bakhtishu, a Christian physician from a Gondishapur family. Claims of an earlier hospital, built in Damascus in 707, are disputed; some historians see it as little more than a leper house.

Hospitals soon spread across the Islamic world. Ahmad ibn Tulun, the Abbasid governor of Egypt, built a hospital in 872; the ruler 'Adud al-Dawla opened a great one beside the Tigris in Baghdad in 981 or 982; and in the 12th century the hospitals founded under Nur al-Din in Damascus led a revival of hospital medicine. They were paid for by *waqf*, endowments of shops, mills or whole villages given by rulers and the rich. In the 920s and 930s the Baghdad vizier 'Ali ibn 'Isa sent doctors to districts without care and ruled that the hospitals must serve non-Muslims as well as Muslims.

A large bimaristan had separate halls for women, wards for fevers, eye disease, surgery and the mentally ill, a pharmacy, kitchens and sometimes a library. The medicine practised there was the Greek humoral medicine of Galen, not religious healing, and the best physicians worked and taught on the wards; the 'Adudi in Baghdad, the Tulunid in Cairo and the Nuri in Damascus were renowned as teaching hospitals. Hospitals also made a new kind of knowledge possible. Al-Razi, who directed hospitals in Rayy and Baghdad, kept notes on large numbers of patients and used them to test what Galen had predicted.

It is easy to make these institutions sound more modern than they were. Teaching is documented at some great hospitals, but how many held formal classes is unknown, and the bimaristans were charitable foundations that rose and fell with their endowments. Their real novelty was scale and permanence: a non-sectarian, endowed public institution where the sick of every faith could be housed, fed and treated.

myth.tradition: Every bimaristan was a teaching hospital with its own medical school, licensing board and student-kept patient records, the forerunner of the modern academic medical center.
myth.record: Teaching is documented at a few great hospitals such as the 'Adudi, the Tulunid and the Nuri, but the evidence does not show how many hospitals held formal classes, and claims of systematic medical schools, records offices and licensing in most hospitals go beyond the sources.

title: The druggist's trade takes shape

confidence.note: Druggists, a 408-recipe formulary and drugs new to Greek medicine are attested from the 9th century, but no single date marks pharmacy becoming a separate trade. Inspectors' manuals mention the medical trade only briefly before the 12th century, so how far market oversight of drugs matched practice is not known.

summary: By the 9th century Iraq had druggists with their own word for the trade, hospital formularies and drugs the Greeks never knew; inspectors' manuals show markets policed for drugs and weights.
body: By the 9th century druggists (*saydalani*) were at work in Iraq. Hunayn ibn Ishaq's father was a pharmacist at al-Hira, and Ibn Masawayh learned pharmacy from his father before directing a hospital. Sabur ibn Sahl's formulary from Gondishapur gave instructions for 408 compound drugs, and physicians were using medicines unknown to the Greeks, such as camphor and musk. Manuals for the market inspector (*muhtasib*), even before the 12th century, mentioned the medical trade mostly in relation to drugs, weights and measures. Around 1050 al-Biruni opened his book on pharmacy with the origin of the Arabic word for druggist.

title: Al-Razi tells smallpox from measles

confidence.note: Al-Razi's life (865–c. 925) and his surviving works are well attested, though his hospital posts are reported by later biographers; the smallpox treatise and *Doubts about Galen* cannot be dated more closely than his working life. The control-group comparison is a single example in the *Comprehensive Book*, compiled after his death, so its details are thin.

people: Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (865–c. 925), physician and philosopher, known in Latin as Rhazes
summary: A Persian hospital director separated smallpox from measles, picked holes in Galen and counted how often patients failed to follow the textbook.
body: Abu Bakr al-Razi (865–c. 925), known in Latin as Rhazes, was a hospital director in his home town of Rayy and in Baghdad and one of the most innovative clinicians of the medieval world. His celebrated treatise on the difference between smallpox and measles taught physicians to tell two rash fevers apart. In *Doubts about Galen* he criticized the master, arguing that Galen's own habit of challenging his predecessors licensed it, while his working notes, compiled by his students after his death as the *Comprehensive Book* (*al-Hawi*), mixed reading with cases from his practice.

He tried to test treatments against experience. In *Doubts about Galen* he cited roughly 300 of 2,000 patients whose illness developed contrary to what the Galenic method led him to expect, and in one case he compared patients with 'brain fever' who were and were not bled, an early use of a control group. Yet his own theory stayed broadly Galenic. One popular story, that he chose the site of Harun al-Rashid's hospital by hanging meat around Baghdad, cannot be true: Harun died in 809.

myth.tradition: Caliph Harun al-Rashid asked al-Razi to site Baghdad's hospital, and he hung pieces of meat around the city and chose the spot where they rotted slowest.
myth.record: Harun al-Rashid reigned 786–809 and al-Razi was born in 865, so the story as told is impossible. Al-Razi did direct hospitals in Rayy and Baghdad, but no reliable evidence shows how any site was chosen.

title: Al-Zahrawi's book of surgery

confidence.note: The *Tasrif* survives in manuscripts and in a medieval Latin translation, so its content is secure. Its author's life is poorly documented, and sources conflict: a catalogue gives his dates as 936–1013 and the book as written about 1000, while a National Library of Medicine brochure places his work in Cordoba under 'Abd al-Rahman III, who ruled 912–961.

people: Abu al-Qasim Khalaf ibn al-Abbas al-Zahrawi (936?–1013?), physician and surgeon, known in Latin as Albucasis
Gerard of Cremona (1114–1187), translator of the surgery into Latin in Toledo
Lucien Leclerc (1816–1893), its first French translator
summary: A Cordoban physician's encyclopedia contained an illustrated manual of surgery that taught European surgeons for centuries.
body: Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi, known in Latin as Albucasis, worked in Cordoba under the Umayyad rulers of Spain and, by one catalogue's dating, completed the *Kitab al-Tasrif*, a medical encyclopedia in 30 books, around 1000. Its surgical section divides the craft into three parts, on cautery, on incision and bloodletting, and on setting bones, and it draws the instruments it describes. His 19th-century French translator Lucien Leclerc judged him the first author to describe surgical instruments with figures, or at least the first whose illustrated work survives. It was also important for dentistry, with chapters on gum growths and one of the earliest discussions of tooth prostheses.

Gerard of Cremona translated the surgery into Latin in Toledo in the 12th century, and it became the leading surgical textbook of medieval Europe until later Latin surgeries, such as Saliceto's, replaced it. It was printed at Venice in 1500–1501 in a volume led by Guy de Chauliac's surgery, while a book of the *Tasrif* on drugs had already been printed there in 1471. He leaned on Greek authors, above all Paul of Aegina, but Leclerc found him less of an imitator, speaking more often from his own experience.

title: Ibn al-Haytham and how we see

confidence.note: The *Optics* survives in Arabic and Latin, so its arguments are secure. It cannot be dated precisely: it appears in a list of his works running to 1038, and the popular dating to his years of house arrest before 1021 rests on a 13th-century anecdote.

people: Ibn al-Haytham (965–c. 1040), mathematician and physicist, known in Latin as Alhazen
Friedrich Risner, who printed the Latin text at Basel in 1572
summary: A Cairo mathematician argued that sight works by light entering the eye, not rays leaving it, and Europe learned optics from his book.
body: Ibn al-Haytham (965–c. 1040), known in Latin as Alhazen, wrote his seven-book *Optics* in the early decades of the 11th century, during the years he spent in Fatimid Egypt. Against the mathematicians' theory that visual rays stream out of the eye, he argued that light and color radiate from every point of an object and enter it, and he backed geometry with experiments. For the eye he used Galen's anatomy, taking the crystalline humor (the lens) as the seat of sight. A medieval Latin version, *Perspectiva*, shaped European optics; Risner printed it in 1572, and Kepler knew it.

links.note: He took his anatomy of the eye from the Galenic tradition.
Thirteenth-century Latin optics, from Roger Bacon to Witelo, drew heavily on his book.

title: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine

confidence.note: The *Canon* survives complete, and its Latin career is documented by dozens of printed editions. Its completion date is not recorded: it was begun in Gurgan and finished in Hamadan, where Ibn Sina lived from about 1015 to about 1024 (his own moves are only roughly dated), so completion in that window is an inference.

people: Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), philosopher and physician, known in Latin as Avicenna

summary: A Persian philosopher's five-book encyclopedia became the standard medical textbook of the Islamic world and of Europe's universities for five centuries.
body: Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), known in Europe as Avicenna, was a philosopher whose work shaped medieval Islamic and Latin thought, and a physician who began practicing medicine at 16. Moving from court to court across Iran as a scholar, administrator and vizier, he began his *Canon of Medicine* (*al-Qanun fi al-tibb*) in Gurgan, continued it in Rayy and finished it in Hamadan, where he lived from about 1015 to 1024.

The *Canon* runs to about a million words in five books: general principles; simple drugs in alphabetical order; diseases of each part of the body from head to toe; diseases not confined to one part, such as fevers; and compound remedies. It was not new medicine so much as superbly organized medicine, systematizing Galen and borrowing heavily from al-Razi's *Hawi*. Its orderly presentation, and even its title, *Qanun*, 'canon' or 'code of law', gave it an authority that physicians preferred to al-Razi and even to Galen.

One celebrated passage sets out conditions for learning a drug's strength by experiment rather than by analogy: the drug must be free of acquired qualities, tried on a simple disease, compared on opposite conditions, given in a dose matched to the illness, watched for the timing of its effect, shown to act consistently, and tested on people rather than animals, since a lion or a horse might respond differently.

Translated into Latin by Gerard of Cremona in the 12th century, the *Canon* became the backbone of European university medicine. Some sixty editions of all or part of it were printed between 1500 and 1674, and it was still a set text at Montpellier and Louvain in 1650. It was also commented on in Arabic, notably by Ibn al-Nafis, whose commentary on its anatomy contains his account of the pulmonary circulation, three centuries before Servetus and Colombo.

myth.tradition: Ibn Sina invented the clinical trial: his rules for testing drugs are the first modern controlled trial.
myth.record: His rules are careful advice on learning from experience, and they anticipate some principles of fair testing, such as consistency and testing in humans. But their aim was to decide a drug's humoral quality, whether it is hot or cold, and they say nothing of comparison groups or chance.

links.note: The *Canon* systematized Galenic medicine.
Ibn Sina borrowed extensively from al-Razi's *Hawi*.
Gerard of Cremona's translation made it Europe's standard textbook.
Ibn al-Nafis described the pulmonary circulation in a commentary on the anatomy of the *Canon*.
